claims.text: Pre-exposure Q235 steel produced by standard mill processing typically contains localized inclusions such as MnS.
Pre-exposure Q235 steel typically has a nonuniform native oxide film.
MnS inclusions and unevenly distributed processing oxides act as nucleation sites for micro-galvanic cells in chloride-containing environments.
Micro-galvanic cells associated with surface heterogeneities accelerate corrosion initiation in Q235 steel.
Optimized electropolishing removes or homogenizes surface inclusions and smooths the surface topography of Q235 steel.
Electropolishing homogenizes the near-surface microstructure of Q235 steel.
The electropolished surface rapidly develops a uniform, densely adherent iron oxide film with fewer local defects.
Removal or homogenization of MnS and other inclusions minimizes local galvanic coupling.
Surface heterogeneities act as micro-cathodes that accelerate local anodic dissolution of iron.
Reducing local galvanic cells promotes more uniform oxidation and formation of a coherent protective oxide layer.
The coherent oxide layer reduces localized pitting and overall corrosion degradation.
Relative to untreated Q235 steel, electropolished specimens will show delayed corrosion onset.
Relative to untreated Q235 steel, electropolished specimens will have lower weight loss and fewer localized pits after identical exposures.
Electropolished specimens will exhibit higher electrochemical impedance than untreated specimens.
Higher electrochemical impedance reflects a denser and more protective oxide film.
Untreated Q235 steel develops early pitting and accelerated corrosion patterns in chloride environments because of its heterogeneous surface and inclusions.
The proposed protective effect applies at room temperature and at moderately elevated temperatures around 150°C.
The efficacy of electropolishing depends on sufficient removal of surface heterogeneities and varies with initial inclusion density and electropolishing parameters.
